purpose: Design-potential memory for creative, nonliteral, and style-specific part applications. Used for ideation and recall; placement validation applies only to ObjectIDs in current script.
principles: Part names are suggestions; silhouette, scale, orientation, material, clustering, and context determine visual role.
Micro-builds can use dense detail; macro landmarks need connected large-scale structure first.
Use-case examples must be logged when identified from screenshots, JSON, studies, or user feedback.
If a creative use becomes validated, promote it from catalog to part-family rule only when it becomes placement/orientation/spacing behavior.
Broad experimental prompts require divergent exploration, not consolidation of known motifs.
Comfort motifs are allowed only when they have a named role and add visual value.
Advanced glitch-building reads through strong silhouette, connected structure, focal density, and purposeful part families.
Screenshots and in-game review are higher authority than script intent; non-screenshotted weak variants are removal candidates.

use_cases.literal_role_if_known: ABAND_BENCH is a bench/furnishing part; repurposed as table/body element
use_cases.why_it_works: At micro scale, repeated tiny components read as game mechanics instead of clutter.
use_cases.constraints_or_failure_modes: Do not transfer this density to macro facades.

use_cases.why_it_works: The rectangular wall silhouette becomes a book spine when reduced and repeated in shelf context.
use_cases.constraints_or_failure_modes: At large scale becomes texture noise.

use_cases.visual_role: dining table, chairs, centerpiece, food/flower arrangement
use_cases.orientation_pattern: flat tabletop with centered accent cluster
use_cases.why_it_works: A simple furniture silhouette plus a focal centerpiece reads clearly without many parts.
use_cases.constraints_or_failure_modes: Keep centerpiece contained so it does not become clutter.

use_cases.literal_role_if_known: cave plant/stump repurposed as blossom clusters/tree form
use_cases.why_it_works: Color + clustering overrides literal cave-plant identity and creates blossom mass.
use_cases.constraints_or_failure_modes: Needs visible trunk/anchor; unsupported clusters look random.

use_cases.why_it_works: Mood comes from density, color, partial burial, and contrast between structure and organic growth.
use_cases.constraints_or_failure_modes: Needs focal paths/structures or becomes green noise.

use_cases.visual_role: toys, furniture, appliances, small machines, signs, tabletop objects
use_cases.literal_role_if_known: normal building parts become mini objects
use_cases.why_it_works: At small scale, context dominates literal part name.
use_cases.constraints_or_failure_modes: Must be proportionally coherent; otherwise reads as random debris.

use_cases.literal_role_if_known: literal architecture parts used at larger scale
transformation_methods: avoid hundreds of tiny surface details
use_cases.orientation_pattern: large connected bays, arches, pilasters, trims
use_cases.why_it_works: Large forms are visible at monument scale; tiny details are lost or become noise.
use_cases.constraints_or_failure_modes: Continuous trim must actually touch/overlap; large scaled depth requires offset recalculation.

use_cases.literal_role_if_known: wall panels used as curved shell tiles
transformation_methods: use tilt gain if panels read vertical
use_cases.orientation_pattern: surface-oriented rings, not vertical cylinder rings
use_cases.why_it_works: Achieves alternate dome style while conserving parts vs dense `S_ROOF5` tile fill.
use_cases.constraints_or_failure_modes: Vertical rings fail; needs profile/chord math and screenshot validation.

use_cases.literal_role_if_known: worktop/furniture part used as exterior skin
use_cases.why_it_works: A flat/worktop surface becomes a controllable reflective panel when repeated.
use_cases.constraints_or_failure_modes: High part count; requires orientation validation and may not fit every style.

use_cases.literal_role_if_known: roof tile dome vs wall-panel shell
transformation_methods: dense repeated roof tiles for textured surface
wall-panel shell for smoother lower-count surface
use_cases.why_it_works: Shows tradeoff between ornate detail and part budget; choose based on visual objective.
use_cases.constraints_or_failure_modes: Do not cut validated systems blindly to hit cap.

transformation_methods: do not generate as decorative placeholder
use_cases.why_it_works: Requires in-game setup; generated use is misleading unless explicitly configured.
use_cases.constraints_or_failure_modes: Do not confuse with U_PARAGON placeholder, which is a plugin/default object and not in-game decoration.

use_cases.visual_role: modular skyscraper crowns / colored rooftop identity
use_cases.why_it_works: Circular and square deep sea rooms provide strong macro volume for colored tower crowns; uniqueness comes from silhouette, offsets, pods, bridges, receivers, and purposeful detail.
avoid: red lens band repeated by habit

use_cases.why_it_works: Cargo racks read as cassettes when given rails, orientation consistency, robot arms, and drone bodies.
Drones read as architecture when attached to service collars, struts, and a central spine.
Antennas add skyline identity when physically mounted and functionally named.
Preserves high-value variants and prevents study files from accumulating filler.

visual_reference_examples_v40.title: Cyberpunk vertical city street with vegetation and signage
reusable_lessons: Strong build read comes from layered depth: foreground plants, street corridor, midground towers, distant sky object.
Vegetation can soften hard sci-fi forms without losing the futuristic read.
Neon signs and screens establish identity faster than adding many small structural details.
Tall cylindrical/rounded tower masses work well when broken by horizontal window bands and repeating sign panels.
design_applications: Use a limited number of bright signs/screens as focal anchors rather than covering every wall.
Place plant clusters at thresholds, balcony edges, and tower bases to create lived-in scale.
Use transparent/glass or dark structural panels for vertical tower skins; add glowing strips for wayfinding.

visual_reference_examples_v40.title: Night neon megacity overlook with crystals and platform lighting
reusable_lessons: At night, color zoning can carry the design: cyan/purple/red landmarks define districts.
Large luminous crystals or towers act as navigation landmarks and can justify low structural detail nearby.
High contrast works best when there are dark rest zones between glowing elements.
design_applications: Use one or two high-value glow landmarks per district; avoid uniform glow everywhere.
Layer platforms at different elevations to create skyline depth.
Use colored light families intentionally: cyan for pathing, magenta/purple for spectacle, red/orange for danger/industry.

visual_reference_examples_v40.title: Bioluminescent garden bridge with curved rails
reusable_lessons: A simple bridge becomes memorable when the rails define a strong curve and the surrounding plants glow.
Curved pathing can be more important than high part count.
Dense organic framing makes a small structure feel intentional.
design_applications: Use cables/pipes/long thin parts as curved or angled rail language.
Use glowing plants/lights below or beside the bridge to make the path read at night.
Keep bridge tread repetition regular; put creativity into rail silhouette and lighting.

visual_reference_examples_v40.title: Bioluminescent portal/throne with giant flower canopy
reusable_lessons: Overscaled plant or shell-like parts can become canopy architecture, not just landscaping.
A central orb or sphere becomes stronger when framed by radial petals and dark organic trunks.
Symmetry plus reflection/water turns a small scene into a ceremonial focal point.
design_applications: Treat plant parts as structural canopy/petal ribs when scaled and repeated radially.
Use a central sphere/glow as a portal core; frame it with darker organic supports.
Use water or glossy floors to double the visual impact without doubling part count.

visual_reference_examples_v40.title: Macro train build with station context
reusable_lessons: Macro builds need a clean silhouette first: long body, cab/front, wheels, track, and station context.
Repeated cylinders/pipes are effective when they align to a mechanical rhythm, not random clutter.
Tracks and surrounding platform make the vehicle believable.
design_applications: Use large cylinders/tanks/pipes for boiler/body rhythm.
Use repeated wheel assemblies with consistent spacing; fewer clean wheel modules beat many random parts.
Add station/track context early so the vehicle scale is legible.
candidate_object_roles: floor/beam parts as track and platform

visual_reference_examples_v40.title: Pyramidal roof tower cluster with ribs and fire caps
reusable_lessons: Repeating steep roof modules creates identity quickly.
Diagonal ribs and corner caps make simple pyramid roofs feel engineered.
Top fire/glow caps can turn repeated towers into a ceremonial skyline.
design_applications: Use roof parts as oversized steep caps, not only literal roofs.
Add 4-corner or diagonal ribs to break flat roof faces.
Use consistent tower spacing and repeated roof pitch for a unified compound.
candidate_object_roles: wall panels as simple tower shafts

visual_reference_examples_v40.title: Dense laboratory/display room with shelves and illuminated objects
reusable_lessons: Interior density works when organized into shelves, cases, and zones.
Many tiny objects are acceptable inside a display context because the shelf structure explains them.
Lighting strips and glass cases organize visual clutter.
design_applications: Use shelving/display cases as the container for micro-details.
Group repeated small objects by row and color to avoid randomness.
Use bright horizontal strips as shelf separators and sightline guides.

visual_reference_examples_v40.title: Compact neon shop front with visible interior inventory
reusable_lessons: A small shop can feel complete with a strong sign, open front, and detailed back wall.
The interior display is the identity; the exterior shell can stay simple.
Cables and irregular sign blocks can look intentional if they are framed by a clean storefront.
design_applications: For kiosks/shops, spend parts on visible inventory and sign face, not oversized outer walls.
Use an open front or glass front so the display reads from outside.
Use a few cable/pipe accents to make signage feel connected.

visual_reference_examples_v40.title: Split lab/workstation interior with color-coded rooms
reusable_lessons: Two-room composition works when each side has a distinct lighting color and function.
A central column/divider can separate rooms without closing the view.
Backlit panels and consoles establish purpose faster than dense decoration.
design_applications: Use color as functional zoning: red/orange workbench, cyan/green control area.
Use glass dividers/frames to maintain sightlines.
Treat consoles/screens as primary narrative objects.

visual_reference_examples_v40.title: Rustic cottage with terrain integration and stone retaining walls
reusable_lessons: Terrain integration sells small architecture: stairs, retaining rocks, and raised foundation make it grounded.
A simple gabled roof and warm doorway light carry the cottage identity.
Landscaping and path approach matter as much as the house shell.
design_applications: Use rock/stone parts as retaining walls and foundation skirts.
Build stairs and grade transition before over-detailing walls.
Use warm light at the entrance as the focal anchor.

visual_reference_examples_v40.title: Green-lit sci-fi facade with crystal landmark
reusable_lessons: A single saturated doorway color can define an entire facade.
Large crystal landmarks outside the building create scale and destination.
Dark mechanical framing makes bright interior light stronger.
design_applications: Choose one dominant facade color rather than multiple competing accents.
Use crystal or tall glow objects as exterior wayfinding.
Frame light panels with darker structural parts for contrast.

visual_reference_examples_v40.title: Red-lit castle towers with steep roof modules
reusable_lessons: Steep roofs, red-lit apertures, and vertical massing create gothic/sci-fi castle identity.
Offset/stacked towers can look more natural than a perfectly mirrored fortress.
Spire rods and tall thin accents increase height without many parts.
design_applications: Use steep roof modules as the main style carrier.
Use red-lit windows/oculi sparingly as focal marks.
Use tall rods/spires to extend silhouette cheaply.

visual_reference_examples_v40.title: Modern coastal house with circular windows and turret cap
reusable_lessons: A few strong motifs—circular windows, clean horizontal bands, and a cap roof—define the build.
Landscape and trees become part of the architecture, not separate decoration.
A low part-count modern build can still feel rich through proportions and material contrast.
design_applications: Use repeating circular windows as a vertical motif.
Use a capped turret or bay to break a rectangular mass.
Keep wall fields simple; spend parts on focal windows and roofline.

visual_reference_examples_v40.title: Grand symmetric stair hall with ceiling fins
reusable_lessons: Large symmetrical stairs are powerful because of repetition and scale, not micro-detail.
Ceiling fin repetition can mirror stair rhythm and frame the room.
A checkerboard floor gives strong spatial calibration.
design_applications: Use repeated treads with precise spacing; do not over-decorate the stair surface.
Use ceiling ribs/fins to echo stair geometry.
Use floor patterning to define the room scale.

visual_reference_examples_v40.title: Luminous garden throne with crystal petals and organic framing
reusable_lessons: A small seating object can become a scene if framed by symmetrical light, plants, and trees.
Crystal petals or repeated luminous shards can create a ceremonial crown.
Organic foreground occlusion adds depth and atmosphere.
design_applications: Build a central focal object, then frame it with radial glow and plant density.
Use repeated shard/petal pieces in a fan to create a luminous backdrop.
Use trees/branches as a natural arch or visual curtain.

visual_reference_examples_v45.title: Symmetric illuminated gate hall with banners and framed long-view axis
visual_reference_examples_v45.retention_reason: Useful composition lesson; text is sufficient because similar lighting/entry motifs are already represented.
visual_lessons: A formal entry can read strongly with very few unique forms if the view axis is framed cleanly.
Banners and two-color lighting can create identity without dense geometry.
Door/lamp/sign symmetry is enough to make a corridor feel ceremonial.
design_applications: For interiors, establish axial symmetry and lighting hierarchy before adding props.
Use banner/sign panels as large identity markers rather than many tiny decals.
Frame a long view through stacked arch/door openings for depth.

visual_reference_examples_v45.title: Snow lodge compound with glass pavilion, fountain, and long bridge approach
visual_reference_examples_v45.retention_reason: Good environment/context lesson but not status-quo-breaking; document only.
visual_lessons: Environment-specific palette can carry the build: white/blue snow setting plus glass creates a cold, clean identity.
Long approach bridges make a mid-size building feel larger.
A separate pavilion and fountain create campus depth instead of one isolated block.
design_applications: Match color/material decisions to biome when the build is landscape-dependent.
Use approach bridges/paths to create reveal and scale.
Place small landmark features like fountains at edges or cliffs for scene identity.

visual_reference_examples_v45.title: Starship docked between two vertical gantry towers
visual_reference_examples_v45.retention_reason: Anchor for context-driven macro vehicle/display builds: the towers and gantry make the ship read as infrastructure.
visual_lessons: A ship or macro object becomes more believable when held by infrastructure: towers, bridges, service decks, and lights.
Tall service towers can frame a vehicle without needing the vehicle to be fully enclosed.
Repeating vertical light modules communicate scale and function.
design_applications: For any vehicle display, add cradle/gantry/station context early.
Use two or more vertical towers to frame and scale a horizontal macro object.
Use red/white service lights as functional markers rather than decoration.

visual_reference_examples_v45.title: Tiered black/gold temple with roof curls and stacked platforms
visual_reference_examples_v45.retention_reason: Anchor for large tiered ceremonial architecture using repetition, stairs, roof rhythm, and edge ornaments.
visual_lessons: A grand structure can be built from simple stacked terraces when rooflines and stair axes are consistent.
Repeated edge ornaments can work when they are sparse and placed at corners/roof ends.
Large stairs and platforms create ceremony; detail density can remain low.
design_applications: Build terrace hierarchy first, then add roof/corner ornaments.
Use stairs as the main visual path through multi-level architecture.
Use a small number of high-contrast ornaments at corners/roof tips.

visual_reference_examples_v45.title: Dense neon vertical city variant with ramps, signs, and cyan/magenta districts
visual_reference_examples_v45.retention_reason: Covered by existing neon-city anchors; keep as text-only variant reinforcing district lighting and vertical circulation.
visual_lessons: Vertical cities need visible circulation: ramps, stairs, bridges, and balcony links.
Dense sign fields work when attached to clear tower masses.
Cyan/magenta district lighting separates paths, shops, and spectacle zones.
design_applications: Attach signage to strong building masses, not floating clutter.
Use stairs/ramps as visible circulation spines.
Limit color families by district to preserve readability.

visual_reference_examples_v45.title: Waterfront stepped pyramid and canal city
visual_reference_examples_v45.retention_reason: Useful city-planning lesson; not essential as image because stair/terrace principles are captured elsewhere.
visual_lessons: Waterfront builds gain scale when stairs, docks, canals, and terraces are aligned as a city plan.
A large stepped pyramid can act as a background anchor while smaller market/dock pieces fill foreground.
Water reflections and docks add visual richness without requiring extra building height.
design_applications: Plan large landmarks, docks, bridges, and market areas together.
Use stepped massing to create navigable monumental architecture.
Use water edges as natural composition lines.

visual_reference_examples_v45.title: Street-level neon sign cluster with palm silhouettes and high-rise facades
visual_reference_examples_v45.retention_reason: Variant of neon signage/urban density; document only.
visual_lessons: At street level, vertical signs and palm silhouettes give scale and atmosphere.
Bright sign clusters should have dark negative space around them.
A few tall facade elements can imply a much larger city beyond the immediate build.
design_applications: Use sign clusters at intersections and entrances.
Keep some facades dark to make signs pop.
Use palms/trees to break hard verticals and add human scale.

visual_reference_examples_v45.title: Coastal fort wall complex with long hill stair and ship context
visual_reference_examples_v45.retention_reason: Good terrain/city-planning lesson; covered by existing terrain integration anchors.
visual_lessons: A build can feel much larger when a wall/stair line climbs terrain away from the main structure.
Ships/boats and water edges strengthen settlement identity.
Long axial stairs can connect separate compounds into one scene.
design_applications: Use walls and stairs as terrain-spanning connectors.
Add vehicle/boat context to sell location and function.
Avoid over-detailing distant uphill structures; silhouette and path are enough.

visual_reference_examples_v45.title: Shadow Dread Castle video reference with repeated dark spire modules
visual_reference_examples_v45.retention_reason: Low-resolution screenshot; text lesson retained, but not a strong visual anchor.
visual_lessons: Repeated triangular spires can create a dread/castle identity even at low detail.
Roof silhouette and color mood may matter more than wall micro-detail.
Module repetition works when each tower has a consistent cap language.
design_applications: For dark castle builds, establish roof/spire module first.
Use red accent lights sparingly against dark mass.
Repeat one tower cap system at different scales.

visual_reference_examples_v45.title: Macro hydra/serpent creature made from repeated body segments and clustered head detail
visual_reference_examples_v45.retention_reason: Status-quo-breaking macro creature anchor: demonstrates full biological character from NMS kitbash parts.
visual_lessons: A convincing creature build needs silhouette and anatomy first: body path, heads, claws, eyes, and repeated texture.
Repeated small parts can become scales/spines/eyes when attached to a clear macro body.
Creature identity is strongest when heads and glowing focal points are exaggerated.
design_applications: For creature builds, block body arcs and head positions before adding surface texture.
Use clusters of small parts only after the macro form is readable.
Use glow/focal parts at eyes/mouth/core to establish living character.

video_reference_examples_v46.title: Multi-base Jurassic Park / dinosaur preserve walkthrough
video_reference_examples_v46.retention_reason: Level 2 anchor because video teaches zone flow, walkable reveal, containment context, and multi-base theme planning better than still screenshots.
visual_lessons: Theme identity can be established by one unmistakable signature marker such as a large sign, gate, logo wall, vehicle, or creature silhouette.
A large nostalgic build should be planned as connected zones rather than a single object.
Creature/animal builds read stronger when they include containment context: fences, paddocks, gates, viewing platforms, warning signs, and lab/security zones.
Dense interior prop work succeeds when organized by room function, such as lab displays, control rooms, specimen cases, and exhibit spaces.
Terrain, coastline, paths, platforms, and elevation changes are part of the architecture in outdoor theme builds.
Video review reveals movement, approach, pacing, reveal order, and readability over time; these cannot be fully captured by static screenshots.
design_applications: Plan themed environments as a chain: identity marker → entrance/gate → habitat/encounter zones → viewing areas → interior/lab/control space → vehicle/tour staging → terrain integration.
For creature bases, build the containment system and viewer route as deliberately as the creature itself.
Use iconic recognition features early; do not spend the whole budget on background detail before the theme reads.
Use video walkthroughs to validate pathing, entrances, player-scale readability, and light/fx behavior.
For multi-base builds, treat each base as a zone in one scene system and use repeated pathing/lighting/signage to visually unify them.
failure_risks: Without a strong entrance/signature marker, the viewer may not recognize the theme.
Without containment/context, creatures may read as random decorations.
Without clear paths between zones, a multi-base scene can feel scattered.
Dense props outside a functional room/context can become visual noise.
video_reference_examples_v46.classification: Level 2 visual/video anchor; theme-park / creature-preserve build-system lesson

lessons: negative-space portals create strong focal geometry
machinery/conduits should be embedded into wall skins
visual_toolkit_alien_city_canyon_v51.validation_status: not a hard rule; use as design toolkit and validate part behavior per project

airlock_iris_parameterization_v56.principle: JSON airlock recipe is baseline/control, not a fixed ObjectID/count/scale mandate.
airlock_iris_parameterization_v56.validation: Validate chosen ObjectID orientation, visible face, depth, radius, scale, and overlap before using as solved recipe.
